newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian murders down despite Port Arthur massacre.
newsitem.headline: Australian murders down despite Port Arthur massacre.

text.p: There were fewer murders in Australia in 1996 despite the country's worst modern-day massacre in the island state of Tasmania early in the year, official figures showed on Thursday.
"Despite the taking of 35 lives in Tasmania in a single incident at Port Arthur, the number of murder victims recorded in Australia fell by four percent," the Australian Bureau of Statistics said.
In April 1996, gunman Martin Bryant -- now serving a life sentence for murder -- horrified Australia and the world with a killing spree at the Port Arthur tourist site.
The bureau said the number of murders in Australia fell to 311 in 1996 from 325 in 1995 despite the Port Arthur massacre.
In 1996, Tasmania recorded a murder rate of 7.8 victims in every 100,000 people, up from 1.3 victims in every 100,000 in the previous year.
The murder rate was higher still in the outback Northern Territory, at 9.3 victims per 100,000. Nationwide the rate was 1.7 per 100,000.
But while murders fell, violent crime around the country increased markedly.
The number of assault victims rose 12 percent, while there was an 11-percent increase in sexual assaults and an 18-percent rise in armed robberies, the bureau said.
The number of victims rose in all other crime categories, except car theft, which fell three percent.

"Nationally, offences against property -- unlawful entry, motor vehicle theft and other theft -- were far more common than offences against the person -- murder, manslaughter, assault, sexual assault and kidnapping," the bureau said.
